title: Draft, Sketch, and Prove: Guiding Formal Theorem Provers with Informal Proofs
abstract: We introduce a novel approach to leverage informal proofs to guide automated formal theorem provers with formal proof sketches. Our method, Draft, Sketch, and Prove, translates informal proofs into formal ones and enjoys both the logical rigor provided by formal systems and the wealth of informal data.

sections.title: The Core Insight
sections.content:
Imagine you're trying to prove a mathematical theorem. You start by writing an informal proof, using natural language and mathematical notation. But, to make it formally verifiable, you need to translate it into a formal proof. This is where our approach comes in - we use large language models to guide automated provers with formal proof sketches, making the process more efficient and effective.

We use a three-stage process: drafting informal proofs, mapping them into formal sketches, and proving the remaining conjectures.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
Our method consists of three stages. First, we draft an informal proof for a given problem. Then, we map the informal proof into a formal proof sketch, which is a partial proof that outlines high-level conjecture statements. Finally, we use an automated prover to fill in the missing details in the proof sketch.

We use large language models to generate formal proof sketches from informal proofs, and to prove the remaining conjectures.

sections.title: Benchmark Results
sections.content:
We evaluate our method on the miniF2F dataset, which contains 488 problems from high-school mathematical competitions. Our results show that the automated prover with 11 additional heuristic tactics significantly increases the performance of Sledgehammer, boosting its success rate from 9.9% to 18.0% on the validation set of miniF2F and from 10.4% to 20.9% on the test set.

With informal proofs written by humans, our method achieves success rates of 42.6% and 39.3% on the validation and test sets of miniF2F.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content:
Our approach has significant implications for the field of formal theorem proving. By leveraging informal proofs, we can make formal theorem proving more efficient and effective. This can lead to breakthroughs in various fields, such as mathematics, computer science, and engineering.

Our method also has limitations, such as the need for high-quality informal proofs and the potential for errors in the automated prover.

sections.title: Key Innovations
sections.content:
Our approach introduces several key innovations, including the use of large language models to generate formal proof sketches from informal proofs, and the use of automated provers to fill in the missing details in the proof sketch.

We also introduce a new dataset, miniF2F, which contains informal statements and proofs for 488 problems from high-school mathematical competitions.

sections.title: Try It Yourself
sections.content:
We provide a repository with our code and dataset, allowing you to try out our approach on your own. You can use our method to generate formal proofs for mathematical problems, and explore the potential of leveraging informal proofs in formal theorem proving.

We also provide a tutorial on how to use our method, including how to draft informal proofs, map them into formal sketches, and prove the remaining conjectures.
